First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $11,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax{‖}^{2}}=11\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax‖}=\sqrt{11}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{11}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-31f990c5-9445-506b-958c-e6c3b52764dd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-31f990c5-9445-506b-958c-e6c3b52764dd" :answer-field/id #uuid "31f990c5-9445-506b-958c-e6c3b52764dd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ddda3679-2b94-54f4-b126-2775a43b783a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5a97219a-abbc-57e2-b1d2-b514ebfcc818" "answer-7ae8a743-3acf-5070-9428-27ae75be7fae" "answer-679d7be2-afd4-56e4-a222-6d038f0fed97" "answer-ddda3679-2b94-54f4-b126-2775a43b783a" "answer-540c0dc8-bcd9-54af-927a-97418f253efe"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a97219a-abbc-57e2-b1d2-b514ebfcc818" :answer/id #uuid "5a97219a-abbc-57e2-b1d2-b514ebfcc818" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "11" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ae8a743-3acf-5070-9428-27ae75be7fae" :answer/id #uuid "7ae8a743-3acf-5070-9428-27ae75be7fae" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-679d7be2-afd4-56e4-a222-6d038f0fed97" :answer/id #uuid "679d7be2-afd4-56e4-a222-6d038f0fed97" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ddda3679-2b94-54f4-b126-2775a43b783a" :answer/id #uuid "ddda3679-2b94-54f4-b126-2775a43b783a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{11}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-540c0dc8-bcd9-54af-927a-97418f253efe" :answer/id #uuid "540c0dc8-bcd9-54af-927a-97418f253efe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](images/18/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](images/86/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163320 :tutorial/content "We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9c/9c11e176876a767543250d5b18038cae7b14a36a692a6f14474da6b4312a48b9.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](images/7c/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](images/23/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162225 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

"36128875-8025-5e37-8397-54d8247d47c9" :topic/math-academy-id 3131} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](images/86/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b6f73158-b78c-5262-bb9d-a957e3f79fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6133 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$
